# DORA, State of AI-assisted Software Development (2025)

**Source:** DORA (Google Cloud), *State of AI-assisted Software Development* (2025), version "v. 2025.2" (printed in the footer of every numbered page, pp. 2–141; the cover and back cover carry none). The 2025 DORA Report is "presented by Google Cloud and IT Revolution" with named research partners and sponsors (p. 97); the licence line names Google LLC (p. 141). 142 pages; no ISBN or DOI. PDF at https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/2025_state_of_ai_assisted_software_development.pdf, fetched 2026-10-11. Licence, as p. 141 states it: the report "by Google LLC is licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0". Licence string: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
**Scope:** open-nc
**Type:** Annual research report: a global survey (4,867 respondents, fielded 13 June to 21 July 2025), 78 in-depth interviews run continuously from July 2024 to July 2025, confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modelling and Bayesian regression, with signed chapters, signed sidebars, company case notes and anonymised interview quotations (pp. 4, 103, 112, 115).

## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

The report's central claim, stated in the unsigned executive summary, is that "AI’s primary role in software development is that of an amplifier" [V]: it magnifies the strengths of high-performing organisations and the dysfunctions of struggling ones (p. 3) [AR]. The greatest returns come not from the tools but from a strategic focus on the underlying organisational system (the quality of the internal platform, the clarity of workflows and the alignment of teams); "Without this foundation, AI creates localized pockets of productivity that are often lost to downstream chaos" [V] (p. 3) [AR]. The evidence is more than 100 hours of qualitative data and survey responses from nearly 5,000 technology professionals (p. 3) [AP], with the survey run between 13 June and 21 July 2025 (p. 4) [AP].

Adoption is close to universal: 90% of respondents use AI at work and more than 80% believe it has raised their productivity, while 30% report little or no trust in AI-generated code (p. 4) [AP]. Comparing two people alike in traits, environment and processes, the one with higher AI adoption reports, on average, higher individual effectiveness, organisational performance, valuable work, code quality, product performance, software delivery throughput and team performance, and higher software delivery instability, with similar burnout and friction (pp. 37–38) [AP]; the authors note their limited dataset does not make the compared people strictly identical, only alike in the aspects they consider important to blocking biasing pathways (p. 48, note 24) [AP]. Throughput turned from negative to positive since 2024 (p. 42), but instability still rises, which the summary reads as teams "adapting for speed" [V] while "their underlying systems have not yet evolved to safely manage AI-accelerated development" [V] (p. 4) [AR]. DeBellis reads the stubborn results (flat friction, flat burnout, rising instability) as not entirely a failure of the tool but also of the system to adapt around it: "the value of AI is not going to be unlocked by the technology itself, but by reimagining the system of work it inhabits" [V] (p. 43) [AR].

The new DORA AI Capabilities Model names seven capabilities that amplify AI's benefits: a clear and communicated AI stance, healthy data ecosystems, AI-accessible internal data, strong version control practices, working in small batches, a user-centric focus and quality internal platforms (p. 50) [AR]. Without a user-centric focus, AI adoption's effect on team performance turns negative (p. 60) [AP]; AI's effect on organisational performance is negligible on low-quality platforms and strong on high-quality ones (p. 71) [AP], and is "dramatically amplified" [V] where value stream management is strong (p. 78) [AP]. Kalliamvakou frames AI as both "a mirror and a multiplier" [V] that reflects how organisational systems actually operate (p. 87) [AR], so that AI adoption must be treated as a transformation effort (p. 81) [AR].

Alongside the AI findings, a cluster analysis yields seven team profiles that combine delivery performance with well-being, from *Foundational challenges* to *Harmonious high-achiever*, and the report reads its throughput and instability data as evidence that the "speed vs. stability" trade-off "is a myth" [V] (pp. 15–19) [AR]. The report asks readers to treat its findings "not as rigid prescriptions, but as hypotheses for your own experiments" [V] (p. 96) [AR], and its analyses speak of comparisons rather than effects (p. 48, note 20) [AR].

## Part I: Executive summary, community and foreword (pp. 3–10)

### Key findings (pp. 3–4)

The summary's key findings: AI adoption is nearly universal (90% use it; more than 80% believe it raised their productivity), yet 30% report little to no trust in AI-generated code, "indicating a need for critical validation skills" [V] (p. 4) [AP]. The DORA AI Capabilities Model identifies seven foundational practices, including a clear AI policy, a healthy data ecosystem and a user-centric focus, that the summary says are "proven to amplify the positive impact of AI on organizational performance" [V] (p. 4) [AR]. AI adoption now improves software delivery throughput, "a key shift from last year" [V], but still increases delivery instability (p. 4) [AP]. The research identifies seven team profiles; value stream management (VSM), "the practice of visualizing, analyzing, and improving the flow of work from idea to customer" [V], acts as a force multiplier for AI; and 90% of organisations have adopted platform engineering, which makes a high-quality internal platform "the essential foundation for AI success" [V] (p. 4) [AP] [AR]. Figure 1 plots AI adoption's estimated effect on each outcome with 89% credible intervals (p. 4) [AP].

### Analysis and advice for technology leaders (pp. 5–6)

"Successful AI adoption is a systems problem, not a tools problem" [V]: the value of AI is unlocked by the surrounding technical and cultural environment, and leaders should treat AI adoption as an organisational transformation, investing in the internal platform, the data ecosystem and core engineering disciplines (p. 5) [AR]. Most developers use AI to raise productivity while keeping healthy scepticism about its output; the summary calls this "trust but verify" approach "a sign of mature adoption" [V], and advises that training should teach teams to guide, evaluate and validate AI-generated work rather than simply encourage usage (p. 5) [AR]. Platform engineering is at 90% adoption; the data show a direct correlation between a high-quality internal platform and the ability to unlock AI's value, and organisations that treat the platform as an internal product see greater returns (p. 5) [AP]. The seven team profiles let leaders diagnose team health beyond delivery metrics, for example a team that is high-performing but burning out, or stable but stuck on legacy systems (p. 5) [AR]. VSM gives a systems-level view that applies AI to the right problems, turning localised productivity gains into organisational advantage "instead of simply creating more downstream chaos" [V] (p. 5) [AR]. Readers are told to use the research to form hypotheses, run experiments and measure the results in their own context (p. 6) [AP].

### DORA community (p. 7)

The DORA community offers guest speakers, a Google Group, virtual and in-person events, and discussion on topics including leadership, team empowerment and the evolution of technology practices (p. 7) [AP].

### Foreword: Gene Kim (pp. 8–10)

Kim, signed as "Researcher, Vibe Coder" [V] and co-author of *Vibe Coding*, *The Phoenix Project*, *DevOps Handbook* and *Accelerate*, writes that in 2013 he worked with Dr. Nicole Forsgren and Jez Humble on the State of DevOps research, which became the basis for the DevOps Research and Assessment group (DORA), part of Google Cloud since 2018 (p. 8) [AP]. A little over a decade ago, Kim recalls, deployments were dangerous, complex and full of manual steps, which is why "we only dared to do them once per year" [V]; the 2013 research showed multiple deployments a day were feasible, that reliability seemed to require smaller and more frequent deployments, and that what was needed was great technical practices (automated builds, testing and deployments, proactive production telemetry), an architecture that enabled "independence of action" [V], and a culture of learning (p. 8) [AR].

The data in the 2024 DORA report suggested that the more AI was used, the worse software delivery stability and throughput became; Kim named this "the DORA 2024 anomaly" [V], an "exciting mystery to be solved" [V] (p. 9) [AR]. He has seen AI cause silently deleted tests, broken functionality and deleted production data, and also massively improve outcomes (p. 9) [AE]. With Steve Yegge he wrote *Vibe Coding*, which defines vibe coding as any form of coding where you don't type out code by hand, so that code "emerges from an iterative conversation with an AI" [V]; they credit it with helping them build faster, pursue more ambitious projects, work more autonomously, have more fun and explore a larger option space, "FAAFO!" [V] (p. 9) [AP]. They concluded that failures came from engineering instincts that were now "woefully insufficient" [V] (p. 9) [AR], illustrated by someone used to walking at four miles an hour being asked to drive at 50 without practice (p. 9) [AE]. When AI accelerates development, "our control systems—that’s us—must also speed up" [V], with a footnote citing the Nyquist stability criterion's requirement that a control system run at least twice as fast as the system it controls (pp. 9–10) [AR] [BT]. Kim lists three needs: faster feedback loops, architectures that give independence of action, and a climate for learning given AI's idiosyncratic nature and rapid advance (p. 9) [AR].

Two case studies from *Vibe Coding* follow (p. 10) [BT]. At Adidas, Fernando Cornago's gen AI pilot found teams in loosely coupled architectures with fast feedback loops "experienced productivity gains of 20% to 30%" [V] (measured by commits, pull requests and feature-delivery velocity) and a 50% increase in "Happy Time" [V], while teams tightly coupled to ERP systems saw little or no benefit (p. 10) [AE] [BT]. At Booking.com, Bruno Passos's team found uneven uptake until they realised "the missing ingredient was training" [V]; developers who learned to give more explicit instructions and context saw up to 30% increases in merge requests and higher job satisfaction (p. 10) [AE] [BT]. Kim reads both as pointing to the possibility that "AI amplifies the strengths and weaknesses of our engineering practices" [V], and expects that those without such practices "will likely have a very bad time" [V] (p. 10) [AR].

## Part II: Software delivery performance and seven team profiles (pp. 11–22)

### The delivery factors (pp. 12–13)

Harvey opens with the moment of release, when software's primary value can first be determined and the theoretical "becomes practical—or not" [V] (p. 12) [AR]; teams also need the capabilities and conditions to sustain the long-term health of those who build and run the application, which is why DORA uses software delivery performance as a focal point (p. 12) [AR]. DORA measures two factors (p. 13) [AP]:
- Throughput, how many changes move through the system over time: lead time for changes (commit to production), deployment frequency, and failed deployment recovery time.
- Instability, how well deployments go: change fail rate (deployments needing immediate intervention, likely a rollback or hotfix) and rework rate (unplanned deployments made because of a production incident).
These apply to any application or service regardless of stack, deployment complexity or users (p. 13) [AP].

### Look beyond the metrics (p. 14)

The five metrics are outcomes: "They tell you what is happening, but they don’t explain why." [V] A low deployment frequency might come from technical debt, bureaucratic processes or team burnout, and the metrics alone cannot tell which (p. 14) [AR]. To connect performance data to human experience, DORA ran a cluster analysis (p. 14) [AP] on eight factors defined on p. 15: team performance, product performance, software delivery throughput, software delivery instability, individual effectiveness, valuable work, friction and burnout (p. 15) [AP].

### The seven team profiles (pp. 15–18)

The names and descriptions are "an interpretation of the data" [V] (p. 16) [AP]. Each profile, with its share of respondents; the pp. 17–18 descriptions are read from the page renders (pp. 16–18):
- *Cluster 1, Foundational challenges* (10%): "These teams are stuck in survival mode" [V], with low output and value indicators, high burnout and friction, and notable instability (p. 16) [AE].
- *Cluster 2, The legacy bottleneck* (11%): a constant state of reaction in which unstable systems dictate work and undermine morale; low product performance, value diminished by ongoing quality issues, elevated friction and burnout, and frequent instability that brings a high volume of unplanned, reactive work (p. 17) [AE].
- *Cluster 3, Constrained by process* (17%): a treadmill; stable systems, but effort consumed by inefficient processes, with high burnout and friction, low effectiveness and limited customer or business value; technical instability is not a primary contributor (p. 17) [AE].
- *Cluster 4, High impact, low cadence* (7%): strong product performance and individual effectiveness and a low-friction environment, coupled with low throughput and high instability that the authors call a significant risk to reliability and sustainability (p. 17) [AE].
- *Cluster 5, Stable and methodical* (15%): "steady artisans" [V] delivering high-quality, valuable work at a deliberate and sustainable pace; low burnout and friction, high stability, throughput in a lower percentile (p. 18) [AE].
- *Cluster 6, Pragmatic performers* (20%): impressive speed and stability, better-than-average throughput and low instability, with average burnout and friction, a functional environment that may lack strong engagement drivers (p. 18) [AE].
- *Cluster 7, Harmonious high-achiever* (20%): a virtuous cycle in which a stable, low-friction environment lets teams deliver high-quality work sustainably and without burnout (p. 18) [AE].

### Speed and stability (p. 19)

Figure 10 is read as evidence for a core DORA tenet, that the "speed vs. stability" trade-off "is a myth" [V]: clusters 6 and 7 excel at both, cluster 1 struggles with both, and cluster 4 is cited for the claim that speed without stability is "a dangerous and unsustainable proposition" [V] (p. 19) [AR]. Clusters 6 and 7 are nearly 40% of the sample, an "empirical anchor" [V] showing that high-velocity, high-quality delivery "is not a theoretical ideal but an observable reality" [V] (p. 19) [AR].

### How do you compare? (pp. 20–21)

Measurements are taken at the application or service level, which encourages cross-functional ownership; the most insightful comparisons are of the same application over time, and "The goal is continuous learning and improvement, not necessarily achieving top software delivery performance." [V] (p. 20) [AR]. Figures 11–15 give the 2025 response distributions for each metric (pp. 20–21) [AP]; the running text states no values from them.

### Putting it into practice: a retrospective example (p. 22)

Interventions vary by application, though common patterns such as long review and approval cycles may emerge (p. 22) [AP]. In Harvey's hypothetical, a team in a regular retrospective notices its lead time for changes rising, perhaps from a dashboard but just as likely from simple observation, because "Precision for these metrics isn’t always required, and teams will generally know how they are changing over time." [V] (p. 22) [AE]. To understand the cause they look at development-system data and find code reviews taking longer; they agree to reprioritise code reviews in daily work and to aim for smaller changes, and to review change approval times and all the delivery metrics "in a month’s time" [V] (p. 22) [AE]. Whatever the profile, the goal is "a mindset of continuous improvement" [V] toward a more harmonious, high-achieving state (p. 22) [AR].

## Part III: AI adoption and use (pp. 23–32)

### Adoption and experience (pp. 24–25)

Storer and DeBellis call this "our most in-depth analysis of AI-assisted development yet" [V] (p. 24). Ninety percent of respondents use AI at work, "a 14.1% increase" [V] over the same metric last year, which suggests AI use in software development "has now become the standard" [V] (p. 24) [AP]. An interviewee says no one wants to get left behind and that it will be hard to keep up without generative AI (p. 25) [AE]. Experience with AI tools has a median of 16 months and a mean of 16.22; ChatGPT's November 2022 release came about 31 months before the survey, and the data show an influx of adoption between late 2023 and mid 2024 (p. 25) [AP]. AI users in the sample spent a median of two hours of their most recent workday interacting with AI, about a quarter of an eight-hour day (p. 25) [AP].

### Reflexive use (p. 26)

Reflexive use, defaulting to AI when facing a problem, is not universal among AI users: 7% always use AI for a problem or task and 39% only sometimes, while 60% use it about half the time or more (p. 26) [AP]. A Sabre case note by Jacek Ostrowski, VP Platform Engineering, reports adoption of gen AI assistants rising to 74% over 18 months, 86% of users reporting increased productivity, a steady rise in satisfaction and reported time savings over time, which the note says suggests the benefits grow as users become more proficient, and only 25% using the newest features such as agent mode; Sabre's response is more training and peer-to-peer knowledge sharing (p. 26) [AE].

### Reliance and tasks (p. 27)

Only 5% of AI users do not rely on AI at all at work, while 65% rely on it a moderate amount (37%), a lot (20%) or a great deal (8%) (p. 27) [AP]. As in 2024, the top use is writing new code (71% of those who write code); large majorities of those with the responsibility also use AI for literature reviews (68%), modifying existing code (66%), proofreading (66%) and creating or editing images (66%); less common are analysing requirements (49%), internal communications (48%) and calendar management (25%) (p. 27) [AP].

### Sidebar: How customization supports developer engagement (Edward Fraser, p. 28)

A UC Berkeley graduate research team used eye-tracking and interviews to watch Python developers with one to five years' experience do two short tasks, one with an unfamiliar library and one interpreting a cryptic function (p. 28) [AE]. Student developers embraced AI for mechanical tasks (boilerplate, installing packages) but largely ignored it when deeper understanding was needed: visual attention on AI chat was below 1% in interpretive tasks against nearly 19% in mechanical ones, and students often worked manually "to retain control and comprehension" [V], ignoring even accurate, time-saving suggestions (p. 28) [AE]. The sidebar concludes that AI may disrupt interpretive tasks by adding cognitive load, and recommends customisation (toggling inline suggestions, on-demand-only modes, repository-level config files and linked documentation) so that AI support matches "the nature of the task and preferences of the developer" [V] (p. 28) [AR].

### Surfaces and modes (p. 29)

Conversational chatbots are the most common surface, followed by AI in the IDE; respondents report using AI less often in automated tool chains and other development tools and platforms, which may reflect AI being less visible in those tools (p. 29) [AP]. Of four modes (chat, predictive text, collaborative, agent), chat and predictive text are most common and agent mode least: 61% never use an agentic mode, which the authors say likely reflects its more recent emergence (p. 29) [AP] [AR].

### Perceived productivity, code quality and trust (pp. 30–31)

More than 80% perceive that AI has increased their productivity, over 40% only slightly, and fewer than 10% perceive any decrease (p. 30) [AP]. A majority (59%) see a positive effect on their code quality (31% slight), 30% see none and 10% see a negative effect (p. 30) [AP]. On trust, 70% express some confidence in AI output quality, including 24% with a great deal or a lot, while 30% trust it a little (23%) or not at all (7%) (p. 31) [AP]. The authors conclude that "absolute trust is not a prerequisite for AI-generated outputs to be useful" [V]; interviewees compared their stance to the healthy scepticism they apply to Stack Overflow solutions, used but not always implicitly trusted (p. 31) [AR] [AE]. DORA has previously published five strategies for fostering developers' trust in AI (p. 31) [AP].

### Final thoughts on adoption (p. 32)

AI use is now "virtually ubiquitous" [V] and, despite imperfections, standard practice for most organisations (p. 32) [AR]. Last year competitive pressure, "fear of missing out" [V], drove adoption, but whether social pressure is a logical motivation is "debatable" [V] (p. 32) [AR]. The authors "caution against interpreting these findings of AI’s ubiquity as an indication that all organizations should rapidly move to adopt AI, regardless of their specific needs" [V]; everyone from individual contributor to executive "should think deeply about whether, where, and how AI can and should be applied in their work" [V], a conservative or permissive approach depending on context (p. 32) [AR].

## Part IV: AI's relationship to key outcomes (pp. 33–48)

### The rush to adopt (pp. 34–35)

DeBellis sets the report's 90% beside outside figures: the 2025 Stack Overflow survey (84% using or planning to use AI tools, up from 76%; 47% daily), Atlassian's 2025 State of DevEx survey (99% save time), a LinkedIn report (88% of business leaders call accelerating AI adoption a priority), a McKinsey survey (78% of respondents report that their organisations use AI regularly in at least one business function), Stanford's 2025 HAI AI Index ($252.3 billion of corporate AI investment in 2024, up 26%) and a 323% rise in U.S. job postings mentioning generative AI skills (p. 34) [BT]. "Widespread adoption doesn’t automatically equal widespread value." [V]; adoption can be driven "as much by hype and fear of missing out (FOMO) as by informed strategy" [V] (p. 35) [AR]. The 2024 report estimated a 1.5% fall in throughput and a 7.2% rise in instability for every 25% increase in AI adoption (p. 35) [BT]. A METR study, which note 8 titles as measuring early-2025 AI's impact on experienced open-source developers, suggested developers slowed by 19% still believed they were 20% more efficient (pp. 35, 48, note 8) [BT]. Other third-party research points to possible effects on cognition and well-being (p. 35) [BT]. The author calls for realistic expectations and more evidence-based work; developers rating AI on the SPACE framework reported mostly positive impacts (p. 35) [AR] [BT].

### Measuring AI adoption (p. 36)

The measure was built to be inclusive (not biased toward any role), data-informed (an exploratory factor analysis lets "the data go first" [V]) and theory-driven (p. 36) [AP]. The result is one factor of three interrelated items: trust in AI output quality, reliance on AI, and reflexive use, read as behavioural, reliance and attitudinal dimensions (p. 36) [AR]. A feedback loop likely underlies it: "Trust is a prerequisite for use, but use is the mechanism for building trust." [V]; since the survey is "a snapshot, not a video" [V] of a dynamic process, combining the items into one factor fits (p. 36) [AR].

### Comparisons, not effects (pp. 37, 48)

Findings take the form: comparing two people with the same traits, environment and processes, the one with higher AI adoption reports, on average, a given amount more or less of an outcome (p. 37) [AP]. The authors qualify that their limited dataset does not make the people strictly identical; they are alike in the aspects considered important to blocking biasing pathways (p. 48, note 24) [AP]. Of course "almost no individual, team, or organization is average" [V], but average comparisons can unearth general patterns that set the context for the capabilities chapter (p. 37) [AR]. A note explains that last year's "effects" [V] are this year's comparisons, citing *Regression and Other Stories* on reading regression coefficients as average comparisons (p. 48, note 20) [BT]; the estimates are standardised beta weights (p. 48, notes 22–23) [AP]. The outcomes were chosen to represent the goals of the report's readers (p. 37) [AP]; individual effectiveness replaces last year's "productivity" [V] label; the measure differs slightly, and the authors consider individual effectiveness a more accurate label (p. 48, note 26) [AP].

### The results (pp. 38–39)

Higher AI adoption is associated with higher individual effectiveness, software delivery instability, organisational performance, share of time on valuable work, code quality, product performance, throughput and team performance, and with similar burnout and friction (p. 38) [AP]. Individual effectiveness, code quality, team performance and organisational performance have held steady since 2024; the author treats them as "a baseline, not a headline" [V] (p. 39) [AR]. Possible mechanisms include handling boilerplate and scaffolding, surfacing options quickly, problem-specific output, summarising disparate information, and higher-order tasks like design, planning and analysis, whose individual lifts may "sum and compound" [V] (p. 39) [AR].

### Stubborn results: friction, burnout, instability (pp. 39–41)

No relationship with friction or burnout, and an association with rising instability, are read as reminders that "AI is nested in a larger system" [V] (p. 39) [AR]. As of now "AI tends to turn up at the keyboard" [V], which may explain why code quality and productivity benefit while friction, burnout and instability, properties of the sociotechnical system, do not, "unless the surrounding system and culture changes" [V] (p. 39) [AR].

*Friction.* Citing a 2019 Microsoft study of process issues that get in the way of a good day (unstable and slow systems and tools, outdated documentation, administrative workload, time pressure, repetitive tasks), the author argues that inefficient processes can negate AI's individual gains, and that more change volume without evolved guardrails, roles and "golden paths" [V] could raise verification and coordination costs (p. 40) [AR] [BT]. For the individual, "friction doesn’t vanish so much as move" [V]: from manual grind to deciding and verifying (prompt iteration, result vetting, assessing code that looks remarkably like correct code), which the author suggests could net out to roughly no change in total friction (p. 40) [AR].

*Burnout.* The findings suggest "burnout is stubbornly resistant to technological solutions" [V] and heavily shaped by work culture (p. 40) [AR]. DORA's own data tie burnout to leadership, priority stability and generative cultures, and a 2017 meta-analysis lists low workplace support, lack of workplace justice, low rewards and job insecurity as antecedents (p. 40) [BT]. Qualitative signals aligned with the work-intensification literature suggest perceived capacity gains have raised output expectations in some organisations, so the balance of demands and resources stays the same (p. 40) [AR] [BT]. An interviewee reports stakeholders expecting more work faster, shorter deadlines, and worry about a hard deadline from leadership (p. 41) [AE].

*Instability.* "Lacking these foundational capabilities can completely neutralize any gains from AI." [V]; a team without a strong delivery pipeline and dependent on other teams may stay unstable whatever its AI use, and AI adoption "not only fails to fix instability" [V] but is associated with increasing it (p. 41) [AR]. The technical capabilities may be more vital than ever, or the evidence may point to a more disruptive conclusion: "These technical capabilities and measurements no longer suffice." [V] and must evolve, be replaced or be supplemented (p. 41) [AR]. Against the argument that instability is an acceptable price for AI-enabled throughput, DORA tested whether AI adoption weakens instability's harms and "found no evidence of such a moderating effect" [V]; instability still harms product performance and burnout (p. 41) [AP].

### Shifts since 2024 suggest adaptation (pp. 42–43)

AI's relationship with valuable time reversed from negative to positive, with throughput from negative to positive, and with product performance from neutral to positive (p. 42) [AP]. The author reads these as people, teams and tools adapting: better models on benchmarks, streamlined fine-tuning, cloud tools that connect private data without exposing it, and people learning to offload mundane tasks to spend more time on problem-solving, design and creative work, which may in turn free time for deploying code and lift throughput and product performance (p. 42) [AR]. Why instability did not adapt the survey data cannot answer; it is likely a mix of where people focus, the salience of constraints and the difficulty of problems, amounting to "different learning curves" [V] (p. 42) [AR].

The conclusion: AI has no measurable relationship with burnout and friction and continues its detrimental relationship with stability; this persistence is "not entirely a failure of the tool, but also a failure of the system to adapt around it" [V], the burden of the organisational systems one is nested in (p. 43) [AR].

### Sidebar: The sociocognitive impact of AI on professional developers (Daniella Villalba, pp. 44–47)

Villalba notes that technology can change mental models (paying a stranger for a car ride, before Uber, was almost unthinkable) and studies six constructs of how developers see themselves in relation to their work: authentic pride, meaning of work, need for cognition, existential connection, psychological ownership and skill reprioritisation (p. 44) [AP].
- *Authentic pride.* Of two countervailing hypotheses (AI automates away effortful achievement, or frees people for work they take pride in), the evidence supports the second: higher AI adoption goes with greater authentic pride, through more time on valuable work (p. 45) [AP] [AR].
- *Meaningful work.* No effect of AI on whether developers find their work more or less meaningful; it may be too early to detect (p. 45) [AP].
- *Need for cognition.* Despite student reports of using AI to "turn off their brain" [V], AI adoption did not change developers' need to engage in mental activities (p. 45) [AP] [BT].
- *Existential connection* (the gap William James noted between one's inner world and another's): AI might reduce asking colleagues for help, but no link was found; it may be too early, or AI may create new chances for connection (p. 46) [AP] [BT].
- *Psychological ownership.* With 78% certainty AI adoption is not associated with a diminished sense of ownership over one's code; AI is wielded as a tool, "much like a compiler or a linter" [V], though there is a small, 21% probability, "but notable" [V] in the author's words, that it decreases ownership by blurring who is doing the writing (p. 46) [AP] [AR].
- *Skill reprioritisation.* Asked to rank eight skills, higher adopters rated prompt engineering and, unexpectedly, programming language syntax memorisation as more important; no other skill's importance changed, and the author is "not ready to make conclusions" [V] (p. 47) [AP].
Takeaways: AI adoption "has not meaningfully impacted" [V] how developers experience their work lives; organisations should give developers freedom to double down on valuable work and opportunities to learn to offload toilsome tasks, and developers should see themselves as "the ones in the driver’s seat" [V] (p. 47) [AR]. Figure 29 also carries a label, "Cognitive offloading" [V], that the sidebar's text does not discuss (p. 44) [AP].

## Part V: The DORA AI Capabilities Model (pp. 49–64)

### Building the model (p. 50)

Storer, DeBellis and Harvey went beyond who adopts AI to investigate "the conditions in which AI-assisted software developers observe the best outcomes" [V] (p. 50) [AP]. From 78 in-depth interviews, expert opinion and prior DORA research they selected 15 candidate capabilities; seven showed substantial evidence of an interaction with AI use, meaning that when teams paired them with AI adoption, the difference AI made across outcomes was amplified (p. 50) [AP]. Like the DORA Core Model, this first model will be validated and refined (p. 50) [AP].

### Clear and communicated AI stance (pp. 51–53)

The capability is the comprehensibility and awareness of an organisation's official position on how developers are expected and permitted to use AI tools, measured by four indicators: AI use feels expected, experimentation is supported, permitted tools are clear, and the policy applies to them (p. 51) [AP]. With a high degree of certainty, such a stance amplifies AI's positive influence on individual effectiveness and on organisational performance and turns AI's neutral effect on friction into a decrease; with less certainty it amplifies throughput (p. 52) [AP]. Interviewees routinely lacked clarity about their organisation's stance, which the authors say is likely to show up as some developers acting too conservatively and others too permissively: "Neither of these cases is optimal." [V] (p. 53) [AR]. An interviewee describes hesitating to explore AI over stigma and uncertainty about whether it was encouraged, not wanting to use it in secret either, under a policy concerned mainly with client confidentiality (p. 53) [AE]. The capability measures clarity and awareness, "not the specific content" [V], of the stance, so organisations can set their own (p. 53) [AR].

### Healthy data ecosystems (p. 54)

Measured as the quality, accessibility and unification (not siloed) of internal data; with high certainty it amplifies AI's positive influence on organisational performance, so the saying that AI models are only as good as their data appears to apply "at a local, organizational level" [V] (p. 54) [AP] [AR].

### AI-accessible internal data (pp. 55–56)

Measured by four indicators of AI tools' access to and use of internal company information; with high certainty it amplifies AI's influence on individual effectiveness and code quality (p. 55) [AP]. Gaining these benefits may need "a deeper investment than simply procuring AI licenses" [V]; "if AI can’t access internal company data, how useful can it really be?" [V] (p. 55) [AR]. An interviewee says many clients' data are not organised well enough for AI (p. 56) [AE].

### Strong version control practices (pp. 56–57)

With high certainty, frequent commits amplify AI's influence on individual effectiveness, and more frequent use of rollback or revert amplifies its influence on team performance (p. 56) [AP]. Mature version control works as a "psychological safety net" [V] that lets teams experiment knowing they can revert to a stable state (p. 56) [AR]. The authors have hypothesised that AI's association with higher software instability is likely, in part, because larger batches of code are harder to review (p. 57) [AR]. Separately, although rollback reliance does not directly reduce instability, they suspect its positive effect on team performance for AI-assisted teams may relate to being able to rapidly undo changes when working with larger batches of code and the instability those batches can produce (p. 57) [AR].

### Working in small batches (p. 58)

Measured by lines per commit, changes per release and time to complete a task; with high certainty it amplifies AI's influence on product performance and turns AI's neutral effect on friction into a decrease, while slightly reducing AI's benefit to individual effectiveness (p. 58) [AP]. That reduction supports the authors' theory that AI raises perceived individual effectiveness mainly by helping developers generate a lot of code quickly (p. 58) [AR]. They argue that "individual effectiveness should not necessarily be pursued as a goal in and of itself" [V] but as a means to organisational, team and product performance and well-being, and judge the net effect of small batches positive (p. 58) [AR].

### User-centric focus (pp. 60–61)

Measured by three seven-point Likert items (creating value for users is the focus; users' experience is the top priority; focusing on the user is key to business success); with high certainty it amplifies AI's influence on team performance, and in its absence AI adoption has a negative impact on team performance (p. 60) [AP]. "Without a user-centric focus, AI adoption is unlikely to help teams. It may even harm them." [V] (p. 60) [AR]. DORA has long held that user experience serves as a "North Star" [V] for shared goals (p. 60) [AR]. An interviewee describes meaning drawn from helping many users (p. 60) [AE], and a quotation without attribution reports learning that clinicians need less noise rather than more tools (p. 61) [AE].

### Quality internal platforms (p. 62)

Platforms are capabilities shared across applications, scored by how many of 12 characteristics a respondent's platform has (p. 62) [AP]. With high certainty, quality platforms amplify AI's influence on organisational performance, but they turn AI's neutral effect on friction harmful (p. 62) [AP]. The authors hypothesise that, with no standard best practices yet for AI tools, platforms mainly limit undesired capabilities, "preventing inappropriate use" [V], which may raise friction for heavy adopters without being bad for the organisation (p. 62) [AR].

### Putting the model into practice (pp. 63–64)

Leveraging AI "is not as simple as just adopting new tools" [V] (p. 63) [AR]. The practical advice, one item per capability (p. 64) [AR]: clarify and socialise AI policies, since "Ambiguity around AI stifles adoption and creates risk." [V]; treat data as a strategic asset; connect AI to internal context, beyond buying licences; embrace and fortify safety nets by becoming highly proficient at rollback and revert; reduce the size of work items and "focus on outcomes" [V]; centre users' needs in product strategy, since without that focus developers "may be moving quickly in the wrong direction" [V]; and invest in the internal platform as the guardrails and shared capabilities that let AI benefits scale.

## Part VI: Platform engineering (pp. 65–72)

### Key findings (pp. 66–67)

Maxwell and Good recall that the 2024 report found platforms improved organisational performance and productivity at the cost of more instability and lower throughput (p. 66) [BT]. This year users perceive their platform as a single entity, whose overall effectiveness matters more than any one feature (p. 66) [AR]. Key findings: adoption is 90%; dedicated platform teams are 76%, shifting the challenge to governing a multi-team landscape; a high-quality platform amplifies AI's effect on organisational performance and improves performance, productivity and team well-being; and it enables speed and experimentation with a small but credible rise in instability, "a manageable tradeoff for higher performance overall" [V] (p. 66) [AP] [AR]. Of organisations, 29% use multiple platforms and 29% of respondents work where there are several platform teams, which the authors read as federated, specialised platforms rather than redundancy; leaders now face "governing a complex platform of platforms" [V], helped by loosely coupled teams with clear charters and interfaces (p. 67) [AP] [AR].

### The experience gap and the single entity (pp. 67–69)

Core technical capabilities (reliability, security) are rated well provided while user-experience features (acting on feedback, automation) lag slightly (p. 67) [AP]. A developer's overall impression colours every feature rating, so respondents experience the platform "as a single entity" [V] (p. 68) [AR]. The authors name three pitfalls that a platform-as-product mindset avoids (p. 68) [AR]:
- *Build it and they will come:* building without user research, leaving a "ghost town" [V].
- *The ticket-ops trap:* a reactive "vending machine for infrastructure" [V] with no roadmap, fixed by self-service and golden paths.
- *The ivory tower platform:* a central team dictating tools without feedback, which breeds shadow IT; fixed by a product manager who treats developers as customers and offers paved roads that are "not necessarily mandatory" [V].
Clear feedback on tasks is the capability most correlated with a positive experience, a clean UI correlates less, and both rate among the lowest; "focusing on improving a single capability in isolation is a flawed strategy" [V], and a technically excellent platform that is not user-centric "cannot be considered a success" [V] (p. 69) [AR].

### Force multiplier and risk (pp. 70–72)

A high-quality platform is linked to higher organisational performance, product performance and productivity, and, consistent with past research, to a small but credible rise in instability (higher change failure rate and rework) (p. 70) [AP]. The authors read this as possibly a healthy high-velocity system and a form of "risk compensation" [V], where the platform makes recovery fast and cheap and teams accept more minor failures in pursuit of speed (p. 70) [AR]. AI adoption has a negligible effect on organisational performance when platform quality is low and a strong positive effect when it is high (p. 71) [AP]. A Wayfair quotation reports the biggest gains came from reducing the effort to fix failures, with developers engaging most with targeted, explainable suggestions and auto-generated fixes delivered in their existing tools (p. 71) [AE].

The platform serves AI twice: as the distribution and governance layer that scales AI gains beyond "disconnected local optimizations" [V], and as a risk mitigator and safe space for learning and experimentation, applying the same automated testing and deployment to hand- and AI-written code (p. 72) [AR]. The authors also caution against over-standardising AI practices while AI changes fast (p. 72) [AR]. AI investment without matching platform investment is "unlikely to yield significant returns at the organizational level" [V] (p. 72) [AR]. Three imperatives close the chapter: embrace the holistic experience ("You can’t fix a bad platform by improving one feature." [V]), make the platform the foundation for AI, and use it to calibrate risk appetite by making failure cheap and easily reversed, while recognising "the platform does not eliminate the local impacts of that risk" [V] (p. 72) [AR].

## Part VII: Value stream management (pp. 73–78)

### The case for VSM (p. 74)

Edwards asks whether organisations are getting better or just faster at creating features that deliver no value, burning out teams and adding complexity: "The greatest risk today isn’t falling behind, it’s pouring massive investment into chaotic activity that doesn’t move the needle." [V] (p. 74) [AR]. DORA's core belief is that the highest performers become experts in the system of delivering value, with a capability for "getting better at getting better" [V]: understanding their workflow, identifying their true constraints and applying resources with intention (p. 74) [AR]. Teams that focus on understanding their value streams spend significantly more time on valuable work, and VSM is the force multiplier that turns AI investment into advantage (p. 74) [AP] [AR]. VSM is "not a heavyweight process" [V] but a set of four principles (p. 74) [AP].

### The four principles (pp. 75–76)

*From mental mess to shared map.* A complex system is hard to hold in one head; when a team maps it collectively, its structure and hidden patterns become obvious and a real conversation about what works becomes possible (p. 75) [AR]. Start where impact is greatest and identify the primary constraint first so as not to optimise a part that is not the bottleneck; DORA's long-used starting scope is code commit to production, where teams have "the most agency" [V] and quick wins build credibility to influence discovery and feedback (p. 75) [AR].

*Focus on flow, not just speed.* Shift from local efficiencies to the whole system and measure lead time, process time and the ratio of value-add to wait time (p. 76) [AR]. If mapping shows code review is the bottleneck, apply AI to the review process "rather than using AI to simply generate more code" [V] that worsens it (p. 76) [AE] [AR].

*Create a culture of continuous improvement.* "VSM is not a one-time exercise, but an ongoing cycle of improvement." [V]: revisit the map as the start of every improvement discussion; state clear goals and give teams autonomy and the freedom to experiment "without a fear of reprisals" [V]; share learning; and keep a record of each iterative improvement as "a living history of your progress" [V] (p. 76) [AR].

*Build on a foundation of technical excellence.* A well-designed internal platform with "paved roads" [V] for testing and delivery makes high-performance work scalable (p. 76) [AR]. An interviewee describes estimating work as always uncertain and asks whether the team will have to go through a two- or three-week process every time it wants a firewall rule change (p. 76) [AE].

### 2025 findings (pp. 77–78)

VSM practices drive team performance, more valuable work and better product performance, "arguably the most important result" [V] (p. 77) [AP]. DORA hypothesised that VSM moderates AI's relationship with organisational performance, since without it AI's local efficiencies are "simply absorbed by downstream bottlenecks" [V] (p. 77) [AR]; the analysis validates this: AI adoption alone shows a modest impact, dramatically amplified in organisations with strong VSM (p. 78) [AP]. The chapter's challenge: ask the team, "Can we draw our software delivery value stream on a whiteboard?" [V]; if not, that is the starting point (p. 78) [AR].

## Part VIII: The AI mirror, and skill development (pp. 79–88)

### Systems, not sums of individuals (pp. 80–81)

Kalliamvakou finds that "the environment that AI is nested in shapes its impact" [V], and that the seven capabilities are all team- and organisation-level, so the spotlight should move from how individuals use AI to how organisations design the systems around them (p. 80) [AR]. Organisations are networks of interdependent parts whose performance emerges from their interaction; she cites Deming's argument that most performance issues stem from systems, not people, and his line "A bad system will beat a good person every time." [V] (p. 81) [BT], and the Theory of Constraints' insight that every system has a limiting factor (p. 81) [BT]. Faster coding still meets testing and review queues, integration and deployment: "The system isn’t designed to carry the gains, let alone amplify them." [V] (p. 81) [AR]. As with the shift to cloud, and with Agile and DevOps, which delivered only with deep changes to roles, feedback loops and team boundaries, AI adoption "needs to be treated as a transformation effort" [V], asking whether downstream systems, decision-making structures and incentives (to delegate, verify AI output at scale, share knowledge) keep pace (p. 81) [AR].

### Augmenting and evolving (pp. 82–83)

*Augmenting* prepares systems to carry the gains where individual productivity rises but team throughput does not (p. 82) [AR]: AI first-pass reviews and AI input that highlights risks or summarises diffs; pipelines that reduce wait states and add AI-powered quality checks without manual gates; data infrastructure that connects AI to repos, work tracking, documentation, decision logs and communication tools; security practices and AI-aware monitoring; and change management with the traits of transformational leadership, in which leaders articulate long-term goals and support the transition with training, shared practices and realistic expectations, teams get permission to experiment, make mistakes and share what they learn, and behaviours like verification, delegation, prompt curation and agent orchestration are rewarded (p. 82) [AR]. *Evolving* designs AI-native pipelines, data systems, security and collaboration models such as agentic workflows and swarming; the Continuous AI trend treats AI as a living participant in team processes, constantly updated with context and measured for accuracy, usefulness and cost (p. 83) [AR] [BT]. In both, "the common thread is intention" [V] (p. 83) [AR].

### Where to begin (pp. 84–86)

Starting early lets organisations shape their systems "rather than inherit them by default" [V] (p. 84) [AR]. A natural first step is to examine how work actually flows today, a process commonly known as value stream management; done well, mapping the flow of work exposes where coordination costs accumulate, where delays and rework are common, and where the system absorbs or stalls AI's acceleration (p. 84) [AR]. Small cross-functional working groups of practitioners (engineers, product managers, data engineers, operations, security), with executive sponsorship and sometimes an external facilitator or advisor, map the system from inside and recommend where the system should adapt, where AI can augment processes or roles, and what capabilities to build; "For change to take root, insight must come from those inside the system." [V] (p. 85) [AR]. A group might find AI output missing "team conventions, architectural history, or past incidents" [V] and recommend exposing internal documentation, decision records and historical tickets to AI securely, or using AI to find outdated documentation and inconsistencies between systems and their documentation (pp. 85–86) [AE]. Verification, orchestration and workflow design become more central roles, needing definition, support, aligned incentives and training (p. 86) [AR]. The changes need intention, ownership and sustained support, but not "perfection from the outset" [V] (p. 86) [AR].

### Mirror and multiplier (p. 87)

AI does not change organisational systems on its own; it reflects how they actually operate: "In well-aligned organizations, AI amplifies flow. In fragmented ones, it exposes pain points." [V] (p. 87) [AR]. Teams with brittle processes and implicit knowledge may find those gaps more visible than ever, and for organisations ready to look, "the reflection AI offers becomes a roadmap" [V] (p. 87) [AR].

### Sidebar: AI, a skill development threat and opportunity (Matt Beane, p. 88)

Beane writes that in software, as elsewhere, expertise should flow from seniors to juniors: senior developers teach architectural thinking, pair programming transmits tacit knowledge, and the junior, mid-level and senior "three-generation model" [V] builds skill through joint problem-solving rather than formal training (p. 88) [AR]. Across more than 31 occupations he has shown that default use of intelligent automation changes apprenticeship and leaves novices fewer chances for hands-on work: "Experts can self-serve, so they do." [V]; a few juniors learn despite this participation barrier, most struggle, and his early findings in software engineering show the same pattern, with interesting exceptions (p. 88) [AP] [AR]. Many organisations focus on measuring AI-related productivity (adoption rates, lines of code generated, pull requests merged) rather than skill development; the best will "jointly optimize for productivity and skills development" [V], and in some of his research great productivity came only by insisting on simultaneous skill development (p. 88) [AR] [AP]. AI itself can measure skill by linking developer–AI interactions to version control and outcomes, now that labelling costs are falling (p. 88) [AR]. His summary: "Default AI usage patterns are delivering breakthrough productivity and blocking skill development for most devs." [V] (p. 88) [AR].

## Part IX: Metrics frameworks (pp. 89–94)

### Frameworks as the "why" (pp. 90–91)

D'Angelo, Murillo, Inman and Storer recommend using frameworks to guide measurement: a framework breaks a broad topic into measurable concepts, as SPACE, DevEx, HEART and DORA's software delivery metrics do (p. 90) [AR] [BT]. The first step is to define the goals and decisions measurement will inform, since frameworks differ in goal: developer experience, product excellence or organisational effectiveness (Figure 52, an image whose content is not in the text layer) (p. 90) [AP]. Frameworks are the "why" [V]; ask: Why now? How will you act on your insights? Metrics are the "what" [V] (p. 91) [AR].

### Self-reported and logs-based data (pp. 91–92)

Self-reported data (surveys; interviews and focus groups; diary studies) capture subjective experiences such as satisfaction, well-being and perceived effectiveness without heavy instrumentation, but struggle with standardisation, comparability and scale, and are open to recall and social desirability bias (p. 91) [AP]. Logs-based measures (quantity, time-based, frequency) give continuous, standardised data at scale but need observability into the toolchain; it is "a common misconception that logs-based metrics are objective" [V], since instrumentation varies, errors creep in and interpretation is biased (p. 91) [AR]. Frameworks are a lens that cannot fully capture complex behaviour; metrics are ingredients and frameworks recipes, with some ingredients shared (productivity metrics like commits or pull requests) and some specialised (developer well-being belongs mainly to developer-experience frameworks) (p. 92) [AR]. What matters is measuring to hold yourself accountable to your goals and being "positioned to act on what you measure" [V] (p. 92) [AR].

### Measurement in the age of AI (pp. 93–94)

The authors advise careful consideration of what actually needs to change rather than a complete overhaul: keep existing measures as a baseline and add, for example, acceptance rates of AI suggestions, model quality or trust; if the goal is the same, the framework can stay and the measurements expand (p. 93) [AR]. Measuring AI's impact on the code being produced is hard because "we are trying to measure something as it is changing" [V] (p. 93) [AR]. For the concern that quality is traded for speed, existing metrics can be combined with new ones, for example DORA's delivery metrics with HEART (p. 93) [AR] [BT]. Act on what you measure, align with organisational goals, and get leadership sponsorship; "We are not here to recommend one framework over others." [V]: if a framework "spurs your organization into action, it’s the right framework for right now" [V] (p. 94) [AR]. The chapter closes with a PDCA cycle spelled Plan, Do, Check, Adjust (p. 94) [AP].

## Part X: Final thoughts (pp. 95–96)

Harvey restates the inaugural AI Capabilities Model as a first iteration and "a starting point for an ongoing conversation" [V] (p. 95) [AP]. We are in the nascent stages of AI-assisted development, "where early standardization would be premature" [V]; simply deploying AI tools is "not a panacea for transformation" [V], and a user-centric focus is "a prerequisite for success with AI" [V] (p. 95) [AR]. The findings are complex and "at times may even appear contradictory" [V], reflecting a field in flux (p. 96) [AR]. Readers should run experiments, conduct internal surveys modelled on the 2025 questions, treat platforms as products, and share what they learn through reports, communities of practice or conversation "to foster a culture of continuous learning" [V] (p. 96) [AR]. The greatest risk "isn’t falling behind, but rather investing heavily in chaotic activity that fails to deliver meaningful results" [V] (p. 96) [AR].

## Part XI: Respondents, method and theory (pp. 103–140)

### Demographics and firmographics (pp. 103–112)

DORA has heard from roughly 45,000 professionals over more than a decade; this year 4,867 answered the survey, though not every respondent was in each analysis (pp. 103, 112) [AP]. The median respondent is 41; 62.8% identify as men and 19.2% as women; the most represented roles are full-stack developers, engineering managers and back-end developers; the median is six years in role and three on the current team (pp. 104–106) [AP]. Disability was identified along six dimensions following the Washington Group Short Set, the sixth year DORA has asked about it (p. 105) [AP]. Over respondents' most recent five working days, median time spent in an office was 50%, and 800 respondents worked all five days remotely; almost half used Python at work (p. 107) [AP]. Excluding "Other" responses, the most common industries are Technology, Financial Services and Retail/Consumer/e-Commerce, matching 2024 (p. 108) [AP]. The most common organisation sizes were 10,001 or more employees (22.4%), 51 to 200 employees (16.2%) and 1,001 to 5,000 employees (14.5%) (p. 108) [AP]. Respondents split roughly evenly on whether their application is adding AI-powered experiences, with more than a quarter strongly disagreeing; more than half say its unavailability would have a great deal of impact; the median application is eight years old (pp. 109–110) [AP]. A majority of respondents were developing business applications, with roughly even numbers developing for internal and external audiences (p. 110) [AP]. Respondents came from more than 100 countries, most from the U.S., then the UK and India (p. 111) [AP]. Of 78 interviewees, 70 write or modify code, 67 describe themselves primarily as developers and seven as managers of developers, and 76 were in the U.S., given the interviewer's language fluency and scheduling (p. 112) [AP].

### Methodology (DeBellis and Storer, pp. 113–130)

*Survey.* Questions are chosen for continuity with past work, for outcomes and capabilities the industry cares about, for representativeness and blocking biasing pathways, and for answerability; the survey is localised into six languages and recruited through organic channels (including snowball sampling) and a panel that reaches underrepresented groups and certain industries; this year organic responses sufficed and the panel rounded out the sample (pp. 113–114) [AP]. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four flows: AI, platform engineering, sociocognitive aspects and AI capabilities (p. 114) [AP].

*Interviews.* Semi-structured interviews, introduced last year to triangulate, contextualise and clarify the survey, ran continuously from July 2024 to July 2025, also generating hypotheses on emerging AI practices; sessions were about 90 minutes and remote; quotations were re-transcribed by hand, with brackets for added words and ellipses for removed ones, edited "only in cases where required for clarity or anonymity" [V] (p. 115) [AP].

*Statistics.* The analysis is steeped in *Statistical Rethinking* and *Regression and Other Stories*, shown through a simulated toy example (p. 115) [BT]. Step 1 makes causal assumptions explicit in a directed acyclic graph: "All statistical models contain causal assumptions; our approach is to make them explicit." [V] (p. 116) [AR]. Simulated data from a known structure test whether the method can recover it (p. 117) [AR]. Step 2, a confirmatory factor analysis, checks the measures; with samples as large as DORA's the chi-square test is overly sensitive, so practical fit indices weigh more, and a perfect fit on real data would be "highly unusual and almost worrisome" [V] (pp. 118–119) [AR]. Step 3, structural equation modelling, compares the covariance the DAG implies with what is observed, and tests the DAG's implied conditional independencies, "testing a theoretical model’s alibis" [V] (pp. 120–122) [AR]. Step 4 fits Bayesian models on the DAG's adjustment set, read as principled comparisons, with a skeptical prior (student_t(3, 0, 0.5); normal(0, 0.3) for interactions) to tame false positives across many comparisons, since the authors would rather prevent false positives than false negatives (pp. 123, 130) [AR]. The evidence is read through four lenses: predictive accuracy (LOO), sign (Type S), magnitude (Type M) and fit with theory (pp. 124–125) [AP]. Steps 5 and 6 check computational health, predictive alignment and statistical validity, and report 89% credible intervals, a choice that "deliberately shows the arbitrariness of p-value-centric thinking" [V] (pp. 125–127) [AR].

*Author-stated limits.* The chapter does not go into every exact methodological detail (p. 113) [AP]. Its walkthrough is a simulated, simplified and idealised example that smooths over or skips some of the complexity (p. 115) [AP], and the simulation excludes non-linear relationships, measurement error, unknown causal structures and missing values (p. 117) [AP]. The authors interpret the results as principled comparisons, acknowledging the limitations of observational data, and the adjustment set prevents biasing pathways only if the DAG is correct (p. 123) [AP].

### Our research model and its theory (DeBellis, pp. 131–136)

The chapter opens with an epigraph from Byung-Chul Han on theory as a primordial decision about what counts (p. 131) [BT]. The model draws on the DORA community, subject-matter experts, literature and qualitative data, and its assumptions guide the analysis: "Correlation does not imply causation, but our assumptions about causation do impact the correlations we find." [V] (p. 131) [AR]. It is "unique for DORA" [V] in two ways: where the model normally relates many capabilities to many outcomes, this one centres on AI adoption and the capabilities that modify its impact, and the structural equation model only establishes plausibility before targeted Bayesian models give the estimates (p. 131) [AP]. Its concepts are environment traits, service traits, processes and practices (including the seven AI capabilities, out of 15 constructs tested), individual traits, AI adoption (reflexive use, trust, reliance) and the outcomes (pp. 132–134, 136) [AP]. AI adoption "distinguishes simple tool usage from a deeper partnership with technology" [V] (p. 133) [AP].

The theory's pathways (pp. 135–136) [AR] [BT]:
- *Service traits to delivery:* older services often carry significant technical debt; critical services attract attention and resources (automated testing, Site Reliability Engineering) while non-critical ones are starved, creating a drag visible only when too late; AI-infused services bring MLOps challenges.
- *Process and practice to outcomes:* well-designed processes turn throughput and stability into repeatable outcomes, reduce coordination overhead so teams can develop and learn "instead of fire-fighting and stifling process" [V], reduce cognitive load and buffer stress, and help ideas become reality without compromising security, delivery or reliability.
- *Team performance to individual outcomes:* "A well-functioning team doesn’t just deliver products; it carries the individual." [V]; a team lacking collaboration, reliability and efficiency drains the individual.
- *Environment to individual outcomes:* through the Job Demands–Resources model, larger organisations bring bureaucracy and shifting priorities, industries carry their own demands and uncertainties, a lack of resources makes work difficult, and "unstable priorities create moving targets that de-incentivize ambitious, long-term projects" [V].
The chapter justifies the model's most critical pathways rather than every link, a deliberate choice for clarity about its core assumptions (p. 136) [AP]. "This model is our map; we encourage you to use it, question it, and help us improve it." [V] (p. 136) [AR].

### Next steps and appendix (pp. 137–140)

Next steps point to the DORA community, DORA's capabilities and publications, and the books *Flow Engineering*, *Accelerate*, *Team Topologies* and *The Skill Code* (p. 137) [AP]. The appendix gives every outcome's survey items, for example four for individual effectiveness (effectiveness, productivity, impact, flow) and four for burnout (cynicism, burnout, ineffectiveness, spillover into life outside work) (pp. 138–139) [AP]; the three AI adoption items (p. 139) [AP]; and the platform definitions, in which a dedicated platform team "is not required" [V], with the characteristics that make up the platform quality score (p. 140) [AP].

- Nicole Forsgren and Jez Humble: Kim's 2013 collaborators on the State of DevOps research from which DORA grew [BT] (p. 8). Forsgren, Humble and Kim, *Accelerate* (IT Revolution, 2018): cited for older services' technical debt and for process pathways, and recommended reading [BT] (pp. 136–137).
- DORA's own earlier work: the 2024 report (the "anomaly", platform findings, platform as product, burnout's ties to leadership, priority stability and generative cultures), the DORA Core Model, and DORA guides on trust in AI, adoption, small batches, loosely coupled teams, value stream mapping and transformational leadership, cited as continuity [BT] (pp. 9, 31, 35, 40, 50, 53, 58, 64, 66–67, 69, 74, 82).

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

- *A speed versus stability trade-off.* Called "a myth" on the cluster evidence (p. 19).
- *Instability as an acceptable price for AI-enabled throughput.* The argument "does not hold up": no moderating effect was found (p. 41).
- *Reading AI's ubiquity as a reason for every organisation to adopt rapidly.* The authors "caution against" it (p. 32).
- *Adoption as the goal.* The conversation "must shift from adoption to effective use" (p. 5); widespread adoption does not equal widespread value (p. 35).
- *Individual effectiveness as an end in itself.* It is a means to team, product and organisational performance (p. 58).
- *Improving one platform feature in isolation, and three platform anti-patterns* (build it and they will come, ticket-ops, ivory tower) (pp. 68–69, 72).
- *Over-standardising AI practices* while AI changes fast (p. 72); early standardisation "would be premature" (p. 95).
- *Using AI to generate more code into a bottleneck* rather than fixing the constraint (p. 76).
- *Treating falling behind as the greatest risk*, rather than investment in chaotic activity (pp. 74, 96).
- *Overhauling measurement frameworks wholesale for AI*, and the belief that logs-based metrics are objective (pp. 91, 93).
- *Measuring AI productivity without skill development* (Beane, p. 88).
- *Treating the report's findings as rigid prescriptions* (p. 96).

## Citation and source-integrity notes

**Conversion.** The original is a 142-page PDF (Adobe InDesign; PDF metadata creation date 15 October 2025), held at `sources/original/dora-ai-assisted-swdev-2025.pdf` (sha256 `b403c537496ba97e6cf3fff14d5b172f69fd483b173450bd4b7186c7d56f53f8`). The tape `sources/converted/dora-ai-assisted-swdev-2025.md` (13,537 lines, 42,980 words) is its text layer extracted with pdftotext (poppler 26.08.0) in reading-order mode, without `-layout`, so multi-column pages come out column by column. Post-conversion check: 142 form feeds for 142 pages; about 300 words a page; the end (p. 141 licence line and p. 142 back cover) is present; no truncation marker.

**Page anchors.** Page n begins at the (n−1)th form feed. Chapter openers: p. 11 at line 705, p. 23 at 2404, p. 33 at 3569, p. 49 at 5081, p. 65 at 6376, p. 73 at 7248, p. 79 at 7712, p. 89 at 8397, p. 95 at 8879, p. 103 at 9487, p. 113 at 10769, p. 131 at 12589.

**Garbled text layer, and renders.** On pp. 16–18 the cluster profiles' prose is interleaved with the radar-chart labels; pp. 17–18 were rendered and the profiles above are paraphrased from the renders, with `[V]` only on the p. 16 sentence on cluster 1, whose text is clean, and on "steady artisans", which runs contiguously in the tape. Chart axes, legends and moderation labels on many pages (for example pp. 4, 17, 29, 51–62, 69, 71, 78) come out as fragments; this reference records a number only where the running text on the cited page states it; values that appear only in a chart or figure list (for example Figures 11–15, 20–22, 26 and the p. 111 map) are not recorded. Figures 52 and 53 (pp. 90, 92) have no text layer. Figure 29 (p. 44) includes a "Cognitive offloading" label that the sidebar text does not report on; no value is recorded for it.

**Spellings and readings kept as printed.** "unavoidably casual assumptions" (p. 131, where the surrounding text is about causal assumptions). "The increase in performance in spite of the increase in stability" (p. 70, in a passage about increased instability). PDCA is spelled out with "Adjust" for the last step (p. 94). Figure 10's caption reads "FIgure 10" (p. 19). The appendix's platform characteristics list "provides the tools and information I need to work independently" and "provides the tools and info I need to work independently" as separate lines (p. 140). The trust item reads "trust the quality of AI-generated output at work" on p. 36 and "trust the quality of the output from AI-generated code as part of your development work" on p. 139. Cluster 4, described on p. 17 as low throughput and high instability, is the cluster cited on p. 19 for "speed without stability". On AI, p. 41 rejects instability as an acceptable trade-off for throughput; on platforms, p. 66 calls the instability that comes with a high-quality platform "a manageable tradeoff for higher performance overall", and p. 70 a manageable trade-off for its performance gains. Both are recorded above as printed. Rob Edwards is "Application Delivery Lead" on p. 73 and "Lead for Software Delivery and Developer Experience" on p. 100; Benjamin Good is "Lead, Platform Engineer" on p. 65 and "Cloud Solutions Architect" on p. 101. pdftotext joined some line-end hyphenated compounds without the hyphen ("highperforming", "usercentric", "AIassisted"); quotations here avoid those spans.

**Attribution.** The executive summary and the demographics chapter are unsigned; the other chapters and sidebars carry the bylines in the Structure line. Interview quotations are anonymous by design (p. 115). Three pull quotations carry no attribution in the text (pp. 40, 61, 86); the p. 71 quotation names Wayfair within its own text. The p. 98 credits (editor, community guides, advisors) come out of the text layer in an order that does not tie names to roles, so this reference records the p. 97 report team only.
